summary.text: Magnetism is the set of effects that arise through a magnetic field, letting objects pull toward or push away from each other.
Electric currents and the magnetic moments of tiny particles both create magnetic fields, which makes magnetism one half of electromagnetism.
Everyday magnets work through iron, cobalt, nickel and their alloys, but every substance shows some kind of magnetism, usually too faint to feel.

facts.label: Everyday magnetic metals
facts.value: Iron, cobalt, nickel and their alloys

facts.label: Origin of the word
facts.value: Greek for the Magnesian stone, lodestone

facts.label: Oersted's accident, 1820
facts.value: A twitching compass needle showed currents make magnetic fields

facts.label: Gilbert's conclusion, 1600
facts.value: The Earth itself is magnetic, so compasses point north

facts.label: Faraday's discovery, 1831
facts.value: A changing magnetic flux induces a voltage in a wire loop

items.prompt: A magnet hangs over a pile of aluminium foil and a steel paperclip. Only the paperclip jumps up. What best explains why the foil seems unaffected?

options.label: Foil has no magnetism at all, so nothing can act on it
Foil responds, but so weakly that you cannot feel it
Foil is too thin for a magnetic field to reach it
Foil is repelled so strongly that it hides the effect

items.explain: All substances show some magnetism. Aluminium is only weakly attracted, so the pull is too small to notice without lab instruments.

items.prompt: Which kind of material gives you the magnets that stick to a fridge door, and why?

options.label: A ferromagnetic one, which can be magnetized and then makes its own field
A diamagnetic one, which is slightly pushed away by any field
A paramagnetic one, which is weakly pulled in by a field
Any metal, because all metals hold a charge permanently

items.explain: Ferromagnetic materials are strongly attracted by fields and can be magnetized into permanent magnets that produce fields themselves.

items.prompt: Early sailors thought a compass needle was drawn to the pole star or a magnetic island. What did William Gilbert's model-earth experiments suggest instead?

options.label: The needle follows the pull of the Sun across the sky
The needle is steered by winds blowing over the sea
The needle is drawn to ice caps at the poles
The needle points north because the whole Earth is magnetic

items.explain: Gilbert's terrella experiments led him to conclude that the Earth itself is magnetic, which is why compasses point north.

items.prompt: A curious physicist waves a compass near a wire and sees the needle twitch the moment a battery is attached. What does this reveal?

options.label: The battery has turned the wire into a lodestone
A flowing current creates a magnetic field around the wire
The compass needle is being heated and expands
The wire is attracting the needle with static electricity

items.explain: This is Oersted's finding: an electric current can create a magnetic field, linking electricity and magnetism.

items.prompt: Why do scientists group magnetism and electricity together under one name, electromagnetism?

options.label: Magnets are always powered by a battery inside
Both only work on metals that conduct heat
Currents and particle magnetic moments both produce magnetic fields
Both were first described by the same ancient Greek

items.explain: Because moving charges and the magnetic moments of elementary particles both give rise to magnetic fields, magnetism is one of two aspects of electromagnetism.

items.prompt: You move away from a bar magnet across the room. What happens to the strength of its field where you stand?

options.label: It stays the same, since fields have no range
It grows, because the field spreads out around you
It decreases the farther you are from the source
It flips direction once you pass a certain distance

items.explain: Far from a localized magnetic source, the field decreases with distance.
